ゆき の よる の からさわぎ — False Alarm on a Snowy Night
You say what “might” happen (～かもしれない), what you feel “must” be so (～に ちがいない) and review guesses with でしょう / だろう; on a snowy night when Ana has pains and heads to the hospital.
The baby might be born today.
They might not be real contractions yet.
This child is surely going to be born early.
It’s snowing, so the taxi will probably be late.
It was a false alarm, but next time it might be the real thing.
To form ～かもしれない / ～かもしれません with verbs, い and な adjectives and nouns (without だ!).
To express a strong conviction with ～に ちがいない and tell it apart from ～はず だ (ch. 41).
To review でしょう / だろう (ch. 18): a guess and “right?” (with rising intonation).
To place things on a certainty scale: ～に ちがいない, ～はず だ, ～でしょう, ～かもしれない, together with きっと, たぶん, もしかしたら.

The night of 29 to 30 December. It has snowed all day in Bucharest. Ana is in her 38th week; Carmen, who came for Christmas, is sleeping in the living room. At two o’clock Ana wakes Mihai up. Carmen speaks Spanish with them, and Cristina (a nurse, one of Ana’s students in her Spanish class) also speaks Spanish on the phone; the lines are given in Japanese.
Mihai, wake up. My tummy hurts. …The baby might be coming.
What?! (Looking at the clock) It’s two o’clock. Since when?
For about an hour. Every now and then my belly goes hard and it hurts.
Calm down. I’m a doctor, but not an obstetrician… First, let’s time the gaps between the pains.
(Opening the door) What’s happened? …I knew it! She’s definitely having the baby! Didn’t I tell you?
Mum, we don’t know yet. They might not be real contractions.
But she’s my daughter. I had her early too. It’s definitely coming early.
(Laughing) Mum, not that story now. …Ow, it hurts again.
(Timing on his phone) Twelve minutes… then eight… now fifteen. The gaps are irregular.
I’ll call Cristina. She said I could call her even at night.
(On the phone, in a sleepy voice) Hello… Ana, my teacher? What’s happened?
Sorry to call in the middle of the night. My tummy hurts… the baby might be coming.
How many minutes apart are the pains?
About every ten minutes… but they’re irregular.
Then they might not be real contractions yet. But if you’re worried, it’s probably better to have someone see you at the hospital.
That’s right. Let’s go. The hospital bag is by the door.
But there’s a terrible amount of snow outside. A taxi might not come at all.
(Looking at the app) It says it’ll come in fifteen minutes. But with this snow, it’ll probably take longer.
Mihai, your hands are cold. You’re nervous, aren’t you?
(Laughing) …Just a little. Even if you’re a doctor, your own child is a different matter.
(Putting on her coat) Come on, let’s go! We might meet her today.
(With her hand on her belly) Don’t come out yet, OK? …But if it’s today, that’s fine too.
“ni chigainai” = must…, surely; at, in, on
“mite moratta hō ga ii” = better to have someone see you
“~ta hō ga ii” = it’s better to…

ka-mo-shi-re-nai: five even syllables, said smoothly, without stressing any of them hard as you would in English. The pitch drops slightly after “re”. In casual speech it gets shortened to かも (“kamo”).
chi-ga-i-na-i: five clear syllables; the “ai” in the middle doesn’t merge into one sound like English “eye”, but is “a” + a short “i”. Say it firmly, without hesitating.
With FALLING intonation (でしょう↘) it means “probably”. With RISING intonation (でしょう↗) it means “right?”, as when Carmen says わたし が いった でしょう↗ (“didn’t I tell you?”).

かもしれない expresses a POSSIBILITY: maybe yes, maybe no, about 50%. Literally it’s “か (I wonder) + も (also) + しれない (can’t be known)”: “is it so? who knows”. It goes after the plain form (dictionary, past, negative), but with な adjectives and nouns だ DISAPPEARS.
Tomorrow it might be even colder.
ふあん (without だ) + かもしれない
じんつう (without だ) + かもしれない
Polite: ～かもしれません (Cristina on the phone, Mihai to his mother-in-law). Casual and very common in speech: just かも — うまれる かも! (“the baby might be coming!”).
✗ ふあん だ かもしれない, ✗ じんつう だ かもしれない. だ doesn’t appear before かもしれない. In the past, however, it stays: じんつう だった かもしれない (“they might have been contractions”).

In English: “might”, “may”, “maybe”, “perhaps”. The difference from English “maybe”: in Japanese the possibility comes at the END of the sentence, not at the start. If you want to signal it from the start, add もしかしたら: もしかしたら きょう うまれる かもしれない.
2. ～に ちがいない: “must…, no doubt”

ちがいない literally means “there is no mistake (ちがい)”. ～に ちがいない expresses a very strong CONVICTION of the speaker: “I’d bet anything that…”. It’s formed exactly like かもしれない: plain form + に ちがいない, and with な adjectives and nouns without だ.
She’s surely going to be born early.
Doina must have heard the noise.
The roads on a snowy night must be dangerous.
She must be a child who loves snow.
Polite: ～に ちがいありません. It’s more common in writing and in stories than in everyday conversation, where people simply say きっと ～と おもう or ぜったい ～.

ちがいない vs はず (ch. 41): はず is a LOGICAL conclusion, from facts (“I sent it on the 10th, so it should arrive by the 20th”). ちがいない is YOUR conviction, often from intuition or feeling. Carmen has no calculation at all, only a mother’s instinct: はやく うまれる に ちがいない. Mihai the doctor, who wants facts, wouldn’t say that.
3. Review: でしょう / だろう (ch. 18)
でしょう is the polite form, だろう the casual one (mostly used by men and in writing). Both attach the same way as かもしれない: without だ after な adjectives and nouns (ゆき でしょう, not ✗ ゆき だ でしょう).
With this snow, it’ll probably take longer.
It’s probably better to go to the hospital.
It’ll probably snow tomorrow too. / I told you, didn’t I?
でしょう か makes a very polite question: だいじょうぶ でしょう か (“Would it be all right?”). And ～だろう と おもう = “I think it’s probably…”: あした は はれる だろう と おもう.
Japanese weather forecasts always use でしょう: あした は ゆき でしょう. It’s the “professional” guess, calm, without emotion — that’s also why Cristina, as a nurse, uses it when giving advice.
Japanese has a fine-grained scale. Each step goes with a particular adverb placed at the start of the sentence.
The adverb must match the ending. ✗ もしかしたら ～に ちがいない (“maybe it’s surely…”) is just as odd as in English. ✗ きっと ～かもしれない also sounds unsure; say きっと ～でしょう or もしかしたら ～かもしれない.
Memory trick: もしかしたら and かもしれない both start with uncertainty (“if”, “I wonder”) — they go together. きっと (“surely”) goes with the strong forms: でしょう, はず, ちがいない.
5. Past, negative and ～の かもしれない
All three forms go after the past or the negative without any changes. Watch where the negation goes: it comes BEFORE かもしれない.
They might NOT be real contractions.
I heard the car and thought the baby must have been born.
Maybe what she actually wanted was to see the snow.
The little one might already know the song.
～の かもしれない (with explanatory の, as in ～ん です) looks for an EXPLANATION: “maybe that’s why…”. Sakura: ゆき が みたかった の かもしれない — maybe that’s why the baby was so restless.
かもしれない けど… softens an opinion: ちがう かもしれない けど、ぼく は こう おもう (“I might be wrong, but this is what I think”). Japanese people use it a lot so as not to sound too categorical.
The correct form with the noun じんつう:
Carmen is convinced by a mother’s instinct: “She’s surely going to be born early.”
What does わたし が いった でしょう? mean (with rising intonation)?
Which adverb fits? 「＿＿ きょう うまれる かもしれない。」

アナ の メッセージ — Ana’s Message
In the morning Ana writes in the “Japanese family” group chat (Haruka, Sakura, Kenji, Mrs Suzuki, Mrs Fumiko, Yuki).
Last night, in the middle of the night, my tummy started hurting and we went to the hospital.
I thought “The baby might be coming today!”, but it was a false alarm.
According to the doctor, the baby is fine and might wait until the due date.
My mum still says: “It’s definitely coming early.”
Mihai is a doctor, but he might have been the most nervous of all.
Next time I write to you, it might be the real thing. Stay tuned!

ゆき の よる — The Snowy Night
On 29 December the heaviest snow of this winter fell on Bucharest.
From morning till evening the snow didn’t stop even once. Cars and trams could only move slowly.
Carmen went out on the balcony and took lots of photos of the white city.
“In Madrid it hardly ever snows like this. My friends are sure to be amazed.”
Mrs Doina, the next-door neighbour, brushing the snow off her hat on the stairs, said: “There’s a lot of snow this year. The baby might come along with it.”
Towards evening Mihai came home earlier than usual. “The roads are slippery; I might walk to the hospital tomorrow.”
In the evening Carmen made a Spanish soup. “On cold days, this is the best thing.”
After dinner Carmen tapped the red circle on the calendar with her finger. “It won’t hold out till the 15th. It’s surely going to be earlier.”
“Mum, there are still more than two weeks to go,” Ana laughed. But her voice sounded a little anxious.
That night, at two o’clock, Ana woke up because of pains in her belly.
After talking to Cristina on the phone, the three of them decided to go to the hospital.
Mihai got dressed in a hurry, took the bag and was the first out the door.
The taxi finally came after thirty minutes. The driver was an old man with a white moustache.
Driving slowly along the snowy road, the old man said with a smile: “My daughter was also born on a snowy night, thirty years ago.”
“Children born on a snowy night grow up strong. That’s what people have said since long ago.”
Outside the window, the empty white streets and the Christmas lights that were still on slid past.
In front of the hospital the old man said “Good luck, mum!” and wouldn’t take the change.
The hospital was the very one where Mihai worked. The obstetrician on duty was a colleague of Mihai’s, a kind woman.
“Oh, Doctor Mihai. Today you’re here not as a doctor, but as a father.”
When they put the monitor on Ana’s belly, a small sound echoed through the room. Ba-bum, ba-bum. It was the baby’s heartbeat.
Hearing it, Carmen pressed her handkerchief to her eyes. Mihai held Ana’s hand in silence.
Ana said quietly: “I thought it was probably all fine, but until I heard this sound, I was still scared.”
After about an hour, the doctor smiled.
“These aren’t real contractions. It’s probably the body practising before the birth.”
“The baby is fine. But it seems she doesn’t feel like coming out yet. She might wait until the due date.”
The doctor showed them the screen. “Look, this is her hand. She has her finger in her mouth.”
Carmen brought her face close to the screen: “Just like Ana! Ana always sucked her finger too.”
“Mum, that’s enough of that story…,” said Ana, turning red.
“But this child is surely coming early,” said Carmen, and the doctor laughed.
“Grandmothers’ intuition is often right. But I don’t think it’s today.”
In the taxi back, looking at the white city, Ana said: “This is the city where our child will be born.”
“Not in Madrid, not in the village in the Carpathians, but here,” Mihai replied.
They got home at half past seven in the morning. The snow had stopped, and the sky above the white roofs was slowly turning pink.
Mrs Doina was waiting for them on the stairs, still in her dressing gown. She was holding a thermos of hot tea.
“I heard a car in the middle of the night and I was sure the baby had been born…!”
“Not yet. It was a false alarm,” said Mihai, and Mrs Doina thought for a moment and said:
“Then she’s waiting for a day with even more snow. She must be a child who loves snow.”
They all laughed quietly on the stairs.
Then Mrs Doina looked at Mihai and burst out laughing. “Mihai, your jumper is inside out.”
Mihai went bright red. “Everyone at the hospital must have seen it too…”
Ana sent Cristina a message: “Sorry about last night. It wasn’t the real thing.”
The reply came straight away: “I’m glad it was just a false alarm. Next time it might be the real thing, so leave the bag by the door.”
Elena called too: “Next time make sure you call me as well!”
“It was the middle of the night, that’s why we didn’t call you,” said Mihai, and Elena got cross: “For a grandmother there’s no such thing as the middle of the night!”
Mihai couldn’t sleep. In the baby’s room he sat down in front of the cot under the ubugi and quietly practised Haruka’s lullaby.
He made mistakes many times and started again from the beginning many times.
At the door, Carmen was listening quietly. “The little one might already know this song.”
Mihai blushed a little: “Then she might sing it better than me.”
After noon Ana woke up. “I had a dream. The baby was laughing in the snow.”
“That surely means we’ll meet her soon,” said Mihai.
That evening Ana wrote a list “for next time” in her notebook.
“One: don’t panic. Two: call Cristina. Three: call Elena too. Four: check Mihai’s jumper.”
Mihai read the list and said “number four isn’t needed, I think”, but Ana and Carmen laughed together: “It might be the most important one.”
Beyond the window, tiny snowflakes were gently falling again.

Write 8–10 sentences about the coming week (the weather, work or school, someone dear to you). Say what might happen (かもしれない), what you’re sure of (に ちがいない) and what’s probable (でしょう). Use a matching adverb with each one.
I used ～かもしれない with a verb, an adjective and a noun (without だ).
I used ～ない かもしれない (negative).
I used ～に ちがいない once or twice.
I used matching adverbs: もしかしたら + かもしれない, きっと / たぶん + でしょう.
